body:
Meaning and importance of mountain passes

A mountain pass is a relatively low passage through a mountain range. It enables movement between valleys or regions separated by mountains. Passes have historically influenced trade, migration, transport and cultural contact.

A pass is different from a peak. A peak is a high point of a mountain, whereas a pass is a comparatively accessible passage across or through a range.

Passes of Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh and Himachal Pradesh

PassState or Union TerritoryGeographical association
Zoji LaJammu and Kashmir-Ladakh regionKashmir Valley and Ladakh
BanihalJammu and KashmirPir Panjal range; Jammu region and Kashmir Valley
Khardung LaLadakhLeh and Nubra Valley
Chang LaLadakhEastern Ladakh; Pangong Lake region
RohtangHimachal PradeshKullu and Lahaul
Bara-lacha LaHimachal PradeshHigh Himalayan region towards Ladakh
KunzumHimachal PradeshLahaul and Spiti
Shipki LaHimachal PradeshSutlej Valley near the Tibet border

Passes of Uttarakhand and northeastern India

PassStateGeographical association
ManaUttarakhandChamoli; northern Himalayan frontier
NitiUttarakhandChamoli; Niti Valley
LipulekhUttarakhandPithoragarh region
Nathu LaSikkimEastern Himalayas; Tibet border
Jelep LaSikkimEastern Himalayan passage towards Tibet
SelaArunachal PradeshTawang region
Bomdi LaArunachal PradeshWestern Arunachal Himalayan region
PangsauArunachal PradeshPatkai Hills near Myanmar

Himalayan passes may be affected by snowfall, landslides and difficult terrain. Their geographical identities remain stable even when their accessibility changes with the season or transport infrastructure.

Important gaps in the Western Ghats

The Western Ghats are relatively continuous compared with the Eastern Ghats. However, several natural gaps and passes allow movement between the western coastal plains and the interior plateau.

Pass or gapLocationGeographical relationship
Thal GhatMaharashtraMumbai-Nashik region
Bhor GhatMaharashtraMumbai-Pune region
Palghat or Palakkad GapKeralam-Tamil Nadu regionBetween the Nilgiri and Anaimalai hills
Shencottah GapKeralam-Tamil Nadu regionSouthern Western Ghats

The Palghat Gap is particularly important because it forms a broad break in the Western Ghats between Palakkad in Keralam and the Coimbatore region of Tamil Nadu.

Grouping passes by location

Passes are easier to distinguish when grouped by state. Rohtang, Kunzum and Shipki La belong to Himachal Pradesh. Mana, Niti and Lipulekh belong to Uttarakhand. Nathu La and Jelep La belong to Sikkim. Sela and Pangsau belong to Arunachal Pradesh.

Prelims focus

  • Banihal is associated with the Pir Panjal range.
  • Shipki La is in Himachal Pradesh.
  • Lipulekh is in Uttarakhand.
  • Nathu La is in Sikkim.
  • Sela is associated with Arunachal Pradesh's Tawang region.
  • Trap: Palghat Gap belongs to the Western Ghats, not the Himalayas.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 11, India: Physical Environment, Chapter 2, Structure and Physiography; GCERT, Class 9, Social Science, Chapter 14, pp. 106–113; Drishti IAS and competitive-examination Indian geography reference material, Important Mountain Passes of India, state-wise pass listings. Online references consulted 27 November 2026.]
title: Important Mountain Passes and Gaps of India

body:
The Northern Plains

The Northern Plains lie south of the Himalayas. They developed through the deposition of sediments brought by the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra river systems and their tributaries. These sediments, collectively called alluvium, create extensive fertile plains.

The flat terrain, fertile soil, water availability and relatively favourable transport conditions support intensive agriculture and dense settlement.

Regional subdivisions

  • Punjab Plain: Northwestern alluvial plain associated with the Indus tributaries.
  • Ganga Plain: Extends across much of Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and West Bengal.
  • Brahmaputra Plain: Occupies the elongated Brahmaputra Valley of Assam.

Important relief features

FeatureMeaning
BhabarPorous pebble belt along Himalayan foothills where streams may disappear underground
TeraiMoist belt south of Bhabar where underground streams re-emerge
BhangarOlder alluvial deposits on relatively elevated terraces
KhadarNewer alluvium deposited in active floodplains
DoabLand situated between 2 rivers

The Peninsular Plateau

The Peninsular Plateau consists predominantly of ancient crystalline, igneous and metamorphic rocks. It is older and geologically more stable than the Himalayan mountain system. Its uneven surface contains plateaus, hills, river valleys and mineral-rich geological formations.

The Narmada Valley broadly separates the Central Highlands to its north from the Deccan Plateau to its south.

LandformPrincipal locationImportant association
Malwa PlateauWestern Madhya Pradesh and adjoining RajasthanCentral Highlands
BundelkhandUttar Pradesh and Madhya PradeshKen and Betwa rivers
BaghelkhandEastern Madhya Pradesh and adjoining regionsSon basin
Chota Nagpur PlateauJharkhand and adjoining statesCoal and metallic minerals
Deccan PlateauCentral and southern peninsulaBasaltic rocks and black soils in extensive areas
Meghalaya PlateauMeghalayaGaro, Khasi and Jaintia hills

Major peninsular mountain ranges

RangeLocation and relationship
AravalliExtends southwest-northeast through Gujarat, Rajasthan, Haryana and Delhi
VindhyaBroadly north of the Narmada Valley
SatpuraBetween the Narmada and Tapi valleys over much of its extent
Western GhatsWestern edge of the Peninsular Plateau
Eastern GhatsDiscontinuous eastern edge of the plateau
Nilgiri HillsMeeting region of Western and Eastern Ghats
Anaimalai HillsSouthern Western Ghats

The Western Ghats are generally higher and more continuous than the Eastern Ghats. Large east-flowing rivers such as the Godavari and Krishna cross the Eastern Ghats, contributing to their discontinuous character.

Anaimudi in Keralam is the highest peak of the Western Ghats and Peninsular India. Doddabetta is an important peak in the Nilgiri Hills of Tamil Nadu. Guru Shikhar, near Mount Abu in Rajasthan, is the highest peak of the Aravalli range.

The Indian Desert

The Thar Desert lies primarily in western Rajasthan, extending into adjoining regions and Pakistan. It occupies an area west of much of the Aravalli range. Low rainfall, sand dunes, sparse vegetation and seasonal streams characterise the landscape.

The Luni is an important river of this region. It flows southwestwards towards the Rann of Kachchh and has largely seasonal discharge.

Physiographic regions of Gujarat

Gujarat contains 3 broad geographical regions: Kachchh, the Saurashtra peninsula and mainland Gujarat.

Kachchh

Kachchh lies in northwestern Gujarat. The Great Rann occupies extensive areas to its north and east, while the Little Rann lies towards the southeast. The Gulf of Kachchh separates much of Kachchh from Saurashtra. The Banni grasslands lie along the southern margin of the Great Rann.

Saurashtra

Saurashtra is a peninsula bounded by the Arabian Sea, the Gulf of Kachchh and the Gulf of Khambhat. The interior contains uplands from which several rivers flow outward towards different parts of the coast. Girnar near Junagadh is an important hill system.

Mainland Gujarat

Mainland Gujarat includes extensive alluvial plains, river valleys and the eastern hill belt. The northern and northeastern hills are associated with the Aravalli system, while the eastern and southeastern areas include extensions of the Vindhya, Satpura and Western Ghats systems. The Dang region in southern Gujarat belongs to the northern extension of the Western Ghats landscape.

Prelims focus

  • Bhabar lies north of Terai.
  • Khadar is newer alluvium; Bhangar is older alluvium.
  • The Narmada Valley lies between the Vindhya and Satpura ranges over much of its course.
  • Anaimudi is the highest peak of Peninsular India.
  • The Gulf of Kachchh separates Kachchh from Saurashtra.
  • Trap: The Chota Nagpur and Meghalaya plateaus belong to the ancient peninsular geological block.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 9, Contemporary India-I, Chapter 2; NCERT, Class 11, India: Physical Environment, Chapter 2, Structure and Physiography; GCERT, Class 9, Social Science, Chapters 13–14, pp. 99–113; V. N. Kulkarni, Geology of Gujarat, Navnirman, July–December 1985, pp. 1–2, Government of Gujarat online copy. Online references consulted 27 November 2026.]
title: Northern Plains, Peninsular Plateau, Desert and Gujarat's Relief

body:
Understanding river systems

A river system consists of a main river and the streams and rivers that contribute water to it. A drainage basin is the entire area drained by a river and its tributaries. An elevated boundary separating neighbouring drainage basins is called a water divide.

A tributary joins another river. A distributary branches away from the main river, commonly in a delta. The left and right banks of a river are identified while facing downstream.

The major Himalayan rivers receive water from rainfall and snow or glacier melt. They generally flow throughout the year and develop extensive floodplains after leaving the mountains.

The Indus river system

The Indus originates in the Tibetan region near the Kailash range, enters Ladakh and flows northwestwards before continuing through Pakistan towards the Arabian Sea.

Its 5 important eastern tributaries are the Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej. The historical name Punjab refers to the land of these 5 rivers.

RiverSource or geographical association
JhelumVerinag in Kashmir; passes through Wular Lake
ChenabFormed by the Chandra and Bhaga rivers at Tandi, Himachal Pradesh
RaviHimalayan region of Himachal Pradesh
BeasBeas Kund region near Rohtang Pass
SutlejTibetan region near Rakshastal; enters India near Shipki La

The Beas joins the Sutlej at Harike in Punjab. The Bhakra-Nangal project is associated with the Sutlej, whereas the Pong Dam is associated with the Beas.

The Ganga river system

The Bhagirathi originates at Gaumukh near the Gangotri Glacier in Uttarakhand. It meets the Alaknanda at Devprayag. From this confluence, the river is known as the Ganga.

The Ganga enters the Northern Plains near Haridwar and flows across Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Jharkhand and West Bengal. The main channel continues into Bangladesh, where it is known as the Padma. The Bhagirathi-Hooghly branch flows through West Bengal towards the Bay of Bengal.

Major tributaries of the Ganga

TributaryBank of GangaGeographical association
YamunaRightYamunotri Glacier; joins Ganga at Prayagraj
SonRightAmarkantak region; joins Ganga in Bihar
RamgangaLeftUttarakhand and Uttar Pradesh
GomtiLeftUttar Pradesh; Lucknow
GhagharaLeftHimalayan region and northern plains
GandakLeftNepal and Bihar
KosiLeftNepal and Bihar; flood-prone basin

The Chambal, Sind, Betwa and Ken are important tributaries of the Yamuna. They belong to the wider Ganga drainage system but do not directly join the Ganga.

The Damodar flows through Jharkhand and West Bengal and joins the Hooghly system. It was historically associated with destructive flooding in Bengal. The Kosi is similarly known for flooding and channel changes in Bihar.

The Brahmaputra river system

The Brahmaputra originates in Tibet, where it is called the Yarlung Tsangpo. It flows eastwards across Tibet, bends around the eastern Himalayan region and enters Arunachal Pradesh, where it is known as the Siang or Dihang.

After receiving rivers including the Dibang and Lohit, it flows through Assam as the Brahmaputra. Its main channel enters Bangladesh as the Jamuna and joins the Padma. The combined waters ultimately reach the Bay of Bengal through the lower Meghna system.

RegionImportant river name
TibetYarlung Tsangpo
Arunachal PradeshSiang or Dihang
AssamBrahmaputra
BangladeshJamuna

The Subansiri, Manas and Dhansiri are important tributaries of the Brahmaputra system. Majuli is a well-known river island in the Brahmaputra in Assam.

The Barak is another important northeastern river. It originates in Manipur, flows through Assam's Barak Valley and continues towards Bangladesh through the Surma-Kushiyara system. It should not be treated as a direct tributary of the Brahmaputra in Assam.

Major rivers and settlements

SettlementRiver
SrinagarJhelum
HaridwarGanga
DelhiYamuna
AgraYamuna
PrayagrajGanga-Yamuna confluence
VaranasiGanga
PatnaGanga
KolkataHooghly
GuwahatiBrahmaputra

Prelims focus

  • Chandra and Bhaga form the Chenab.
  • Bhagirathi and Alaknanda meet at Devprayag.
  • The Yamuna joins the Ganga at Prayagraj.
  • The Brahmaputra is known as Tsangpo in Tibet and Jamuna in Bangladesh.
  • The Jhelum passes through Wular Lake.
  • Trap: The Yamuna in India and the Jamuna in Bangladesh are different rivers.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 9, Contemporary India-I, Chapter 3, Drainage; NCERT, Class 11, India: Physical Environment, Chapter 3, Drainage System, SATHEE online textbook; GCERT, Class 9, Social Science, Chapter 15, Drainage System, pp. 114–120. Online textbooks consulted 27 November 2026.]
title: Himalayan Rivers: Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra Systems

body:
General characteristics of Peninsular rivers

The Peninsular rivers drain the ancient plateau of central and southern India. Their flow depends more heavily on seasonal rainfall than that of the major Himalayan rivers, although several maintain flow throughout the year.

Much of the Peninsular Plateau slopes eastwards. Consequently, most large Peninsular rivers flow towards the Bay of Bengal. The Narmada and Tapi are important exceptions because they flow westwards through structurally controlled valleys.

Major east-flowing rivers

RiverSourcePrincipal states along the main course
MahanadiSihawa HillsChhattisgarh, Odisha
GodavariTrimbakeshwar near NashikMaharashtra, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh
KrishnaMahabaleshwarMaharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh
PennarNandi Hills regionKarnataka, Andhra Pradesh
KaveriTalakaveri, Brahmagiri HillsKarnataka, Tamil Nadu

All these rivers ultimately drain into the Bay of Bengal. Their drainage basins may extend into states beyond those crossed by the main river channel.

Mahanadi

The Mahanadi originates in Chhattisgarh and flows into Odisha. It forms a delta near the Odisha coast. The Hirakud Dam near Sambalpur is an important project on the river. The Hasdeo, Mand and Ib rivers belong to the Mahanadi drainage system.

Godavari

The Godavari is the longest Peninsular river and has the largest drainage basin among Peninsular rivers. It originates in the Western Ghats of Maharashtra and flows eastwards through central India towards coastal Andhra Pradesh.

Its principal tributaries include the Pranhita, Indravati, Manjira, Purna and Sabari. The Pranhita is formed by the confluence of the Wardha and Wainganga rivers. The Godavari forms an extensive delta before entering the Bay of Bengal.

Krishna

The Krishna originates near Mahabaleshwar in Maharashtra and drains a large part of the Deccan Plateau. The Bhima and Tungabhadra are important tributaries. The Tungabhadra is itself formed by the Tunga and Bhadra rivers.

The Srisailam and Nagarjuna Sagar dams are associated with the Krishna. Vijayawada lies on the river in Andhra Pradesh.

Kaveri

The Kaveri originates at Talakaveri in the Brahmagiri Hills of Karnataka. It flows through southern Karnataka and Tamil Nadu before entering the Bay of Bengal.

The Kabini, Hemavati, Bhavani and Amaravati are important tributaries. The river supports irrigated agriculture in the Kaveri delta, especially in the Thanjavur region of Tamil Nadu.

Other eastern river systems

  • The Subarnarekha originates in the Chota Nagpur region and flows through Jharkhand, West Bengal and Odisha.
  • The Brahmani is formed by the Sankh and South Koel rivers and flows through Odisha.
  • The Baitarani is an important river of Odisha.
  • The Pennar is distinct from the Krishna and Kaveri and drains parts of Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh.

Major west-flowing rivers

RiverSourceOutlet
NarmadaAmarkantak, Madhya PradeshGulf of Khambhat
TapiMultai, Madhya PradeshGulf of Khambhat
MahiVindhyan region, Madhya PradeshGulf of Khambhat
SabarmatiAravalli Hills, RajasthanGulf of Khambhat
MandoviWestern Ghats, KarnatakaArabian Sea in Goa
SharavatiWestern Ghats, KarnatakaArabian Sea
PeriyarSouthern Western GhatsWestern coastal waters of Keralam

The Narmada flows between the Vindhya and Satpura ranges over much of its course. The Tapi flows south of the Satpura range. Both enter the Arabian Sea through the Gulf of Khambhat region.

Deltas and estuaries

A delta develops when a river deposits sediment near its mouth, creating new land and often dividing into distributaries. An estuary is a coastal opening where river water mixes with seawater under tidal influence.

The Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri form well-known deltas. The Narmada and Tapi form estuarine mouths. This is an important geographical distinction, but the direction of river flow alone does not determine whether a delta or estuary develops.

Prelims focus

  • The Godavari has the largest Peninsular drainage basin.
  • The Krishna originates near Mahabaleshwar.
  • The Kaveri originates in the Brahmagiri Hills.
  • Hirakud Dam is on the Mahanadi.
  • The Narmada and Tapi drain westwards into the Arabian Sea.
  • Trap: The Tungabhadra belongs to the Krishna system, not the Godavari system.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 9, Contemporary India-I, Chapter 3, Drainage; NCERT, Class 11, India: Physical Environment, Chapter 3, Drainage System; GCERT, Class 9, Social Science, Chapter 15, Drainage System, pp. 114–120. Online textbook versions consulted 27 November 2026.]
title: Peninsular Rivers and Their Drainage Basins
